- `spot-check-rmqr` had been broken before this change: its "does it fit behind an ECI header" probe caught an `ArgumentException` that the sizing API stopped throwing when it became `Try`-only, so the first version that could not hold "é" behind an ECI header ended the run. It asks `TryGetRequiredBufferSize` now.
- 6.5 inherits a visible seam: until sets learn Kanji, a text one symbol holds in Kanji but not in UTF-8 comes out as a UTF-8 set of two or more, where `Create` gives one Kanji symbol.

**Trimmed size.** Measured against 6.1 (`27a5caf`, table unreferenced), `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: QR encode only 115,200 → 132,608 bytes (+17.0 KB), all three symbologies encoding 178,176 → 197,120 (+18.5 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged. Almost all of it arrived with 6.2, not here: 6.2's writers put the table in reachable mode switches, and a trimmer cannot know that no analysis selected Kanji, so against 6.2 (`c7ee3aa`) this phase adds 0 bytes to QR encode only and 512 to all three. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md) beside the table's size.

**Benchmark delta.** Base `c7ee3aa` against this change, both trees exported, ShortRun, three rounds alternating on an idle machine, median of three per arm, 109 arms: the 6.2 set plus `KanjiEncode`, new here (an all-cells text per symbology beside the same text with UTF-8 asked for; the class was copied into the base tree, so base runs today's UTF-8 path). Allocation is identical on every arm. The arms that write Kanji now are faster than both their twins: Standard QR 8 characters 1,001 ns at base → 807 at head, where the head's forced UTF-8 twin takes 972; 320 characters 25.6 → 14.7 µs against 25.6; rMQR 15 characters 381 → 319 ns against 382; Micro QR 184 → 183 ns, where base writes UTF-8 at M4 and head Kanji at M3 (Micro QR has no charset option, so base is its only twin). Class medians of the other arms: `SimpleEncode` -0.6 %, `SimpleMicroQREncode` +1.7 %, `SimpleRmQREncode` +2.3 %, `QRCodeEncodeEndToEnd` +2.8 %, `MicroQREncodeEndToend` +1.2 %, `RmQREncodeEndToEnd` +0.1 %, segmentation classes -0.9 to +2.0 %, except Micro QR `Single` at +7.2 %. The arms past +5 % (every Micro QR `Single` shape, up to +17.4 %; `QR_Byte_V40_H_Encode` +12.5 %; Standard QR `Optimal` alnum-120 +19.8 %; rMQR numeric R7x43 +8.9 %) were measured again with three launches of fifteen iterations, base and head interleaved twice, and all came back between -4.0 and +4.0 % except rMQR numeric R7x43 at +6.0 %. With six launches that arm is the same call with the same text in two classes, and it measured +7.4 % in `SimpleRmQREncode` and -0.8 % in `RmQREncodeEndToEnd`: per-process layout, not a cost on that path, whose only change is the analysis call.

### 6.4 `Optimal` learns Kanji (2026-09-30)

**Done.** An eighth state, Kanji, in a program of its own: `ModeSegmenter.ComputeCostsKanji` (a cost-only loop and one with parents) for a text whose characters are all ASCII or have an encoder cell. An ASCII character reaches Numeric, Alphanumeric and Byte at one byte; a character with a cell reaches only Kanji, since Byte would need an ECI header. After any character either Kanji or the other states are reachable, never both, so Kanji's predecessor takes the byte Byte's takes at an ASCII position: the table stays two bytes a character, and `WalkBack` steps a Kanji run as it steps a Byte run (`CountRuns` gained a Kanji count). The seven-state loops and the lanes are untouched. `TextAnalyzer.Analyze(text, eci, allowKanji, planKanji)` reads past ASCII only when `planKanji` is set, which only the `Optimal` paths do, and marks such a text `KanjiPlannable` on its UTF-8 analysis; `Single` pays nothing new. Each planner branches on the mark into a scan of its own, which takes, below the single-mode (UTF-8) fit, the first candidate a plan holds, the Kanji plan (no ECI header) where both do and the UTF-8 plan otherwise, and returns which one to build (`kanjiPlan`); the generators build it with `TryBuildKanjiPlan` and write it under no charset. Weighing the UTF-8 plan as well was decided here, not in the plan: without it `Optimal` would grow symbols it wrote before, since interleaved kanji and digits pay a header per run as Kanji runs (「1日」×20 then 60 digits: the UTF-8 plan is 7-M, the Kanji plan 8-M). Structured Append sets take no mark (their analysis is the two-argument one), so the lanes, which only sets use, never see the eighth state; that is K9 for now, and 6.5 has to keep it so. `PublicAPI.approved.txt` is unchanged.

Bounds re-derived for the Kanji plan, per the inventory:
- `CheapestSixths` → `CheapestSixthsKanji`: a character with a cell at 78 sixths (13 bits). This is the one screen term that decides: at the UTF-8 rate a kana is 144, and the screen would skip Standard QR's winning version for kana-heavy text and M3 for 「日本語12345」 on Micro QR.
- The header term: the inventory's premise was about the narrowest header (Standard QR's `MinCountBitsAny` stays 8, since Kanji's width at versions 1-9 is 8 too; Micro QR's Kanji header is (version − 1) + version bits; rMQR's 3 + 2). One header in all could not decide for a text the Kanji scan sees, since its plan has a run of each kind. The screens now add a header for every stretch of characters with a cell and every stretch of ASCII (`ModeSegmenter.CheapestSixthsKanji` counts them in the same pass), because no run crosses between them; this was added for speed, after the benchmark (below), and it is tight where each stretch is one run at the narrowest header.
- rMQR: the floor runs at 4 / 3 / 3 / 2 (Kanji's 2 at R7x43 and R11x27), and at 3 it skips 「あい123」, whose Kanji plan fills R7x43-M's 48 bits exactly; the upper bound re-prices the floor plan's Kanji runs; the memo key carries Kanji's width (R13x77 and R15x59 share the other three, as do R13x139 and R17x99); a requested version the single stream does not fit prices the Kanji plan there, since the scan has to say which plan to build.
- `QRSegmentPlanner.PlanCouldBeatSingleMode` / `PlanIsOneByteRun` and the Structured Append premises only Structured Append asks, so they move with 6.5. `CanPlanBeatSingleMode` needs nothing: a plannable text's single mode is Byte.

**Verified.**
- `ModeSegmenterKanjiParityTest`: both loops against `KanjiPlanReference`, an all-states relaxation over eight states written with nothing from the library (a character outside ASCII reaches Kanji only, ASCII classed from the standard's alphabet), on 51 eligible texts (fixed shapes, ties, and a seeded random mix) at every width shape the three planners pass, from rMQR's 4 / 3 / 3 / 2 to Standard QR's 27-40 band: cost, end state, the plan walked back run for run, and the runs counted per mode. The reconstructed plan re-priced equals the program's cost, and the Kanji screen is a lower bound at every width. The seven-state suites (`ModeSegmenter*ParityTest`, the lane and Structured Append walks) pass unchanged.
- `KanjiOptimalTest`, through the public API of all three symbologies: the output equals a reference scan (the first version below the UTF-8 fit that a plan holds, the Kanji plan first; for rMQR every version priced from scratch and ranked by the strategy), where a Kanji plan is written out from `KanjiPlanReference` and `KanjiStreamReference` with the mask pinned and a UTF-8 plan is compared with the same text with UTF-8 asked for; every symbol decodes to its text; the version is never larger than `Single`'s or than the UTF-8 plan's; sizing agrees with `Create`, with the boost too. For each bound that decides, a case where the seven-state bound would have skipped the winning plan: the 13-bit screen (Standard QR, Micro QR), no ECI header on a Kanji plan within 12 bits of its capacity, Kanji's own width in each band, rMQR's 2-bit floor at R7x43, the memo key (R15x59's price handed to R13x77), the requested version, and the boost pricing the Kanji plan. The UTF-8 plan kept where it is smaller (Standard QR, Micro QR 「xЯxЯxЯ12345678」, rMQR), and Kanji taken at a version both fit.
- `KanjiPlanBoundsTest`: each planner's screen, rMQR's floor and upper bound against the optimum at every version, the narrowest widths pinned.
- Existing tests that moved, each an eligible text whose output got smaller: `KanjiEligibilityTest`'s `Optimal` row now expects the Kanji plan where it is smaller (only 「東京タワー333m」, 2-M → 1-M), `RmQRSegmentationTest`'s 「日本語1234567890」 goes R11x43 → R13x27, and its exhaustive reference learned the Kanji plan.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 41 faults: in the eighth state's loops (each open, continue and cross-mode transition, the first character, the walk back, the run count, the 13-bit width, the screen's 78 sixths), in the analysis (the ASCII clause, the mark, the sizing opt-in), and in each planner and generator (each re-derived bound, the ECI-free pricing, Kanji's widths, the UTF-8 half of each scan, the plan charset, the boost, sizing). All but two are caught. Both are equivalent in the domain the scans see: `Best`'s tie between Kanji and the other states (after any character only one side is reachable), and Micro QR's screen header at 2 × version instead of 2 × version − 1 (the argument in "Done"). The first pass also left Micro QR's UTF-8 half and rMQR's memo key without a test of their own; the key was caught only where a Kanji key collided with a UTF-8 one. `MicroQr_Utf8PlanIsKept_WhereTheKanjiPlanDoesNotFit` and `RmQr_MemoKeyTellsApartVersionsThatShareTheirOtherWidths` catch them, the second with a key that keeps the programs apart but drops Kanji's width.
- `spot-check-microqr` gained four `Optimal` cases (Kanji beside Numeric at M3-L and M3-M, a text no symbol held as UTF-8, and a Byte run of ASCII beside Kanji at M4-L): 18 of 18. `spot-check-rmqr` gained the largest Kanji plan each version and level holds under `Optimal` where UTF-8 cannot (62 of 64; R7x43-H and R11x27-H hold no Kanji plan), and requires zxing-cpp's raw bytes to be its Shift_JIS encoding: 444 of 444. `KanjiZXingCrossTest` has ZXing.Net read Kanji plans in all three Standard QR count bands.
- Byte-identical: the 6.3 harness, rebuilt against each tree (`e6555a6` and this change, each run printing the assembly and MVID it loaded), with the corpus grown by 200 random eligible texts with ASCII in them and the shapes above: 52,716 cases over 754 texts. ASCII, Latin-1, empty, no-cell and all-cells text: 0 differences in 40,154 cases. Eligible text with ASCII: 855 of 12,562 differ, every one under `Optimal` with the charset left to the library (none under `Single`, an explicit charset or a byte order mark), sets only where the set is one symbol. Of the size lines that moved, 265 went to a smaller version and 73 fit where they did not; none grew or stopped fitting (rMQR compared on core modules, by each case's fit strategy). 16 symbols changed at the same version, where the Kanji plan and the UTF-8 plan tie. The same harness against the tree after the speed work below gives the same 52,716 results.
- The speed work below was mutation-checked on its own: 15 faults in the per-stretch screen (each run count, each symbology's header per stretch, the UTF-8 screen's two-byte price), the analysis's ASCII test, and the hoisted widths and payloads in `MeasurePlan`, `PricePlan` and the two writers. All but one are caught. The survivor is equivalent: it tightens Standard QR's UTF-8 screen by one bit, and a UTF-8 plan is weighed only below the single stream's fit, where it has two runs at least and so costs a header more than the screen.

**Trimmed size.** Against `e6555a6`, `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: QR encode only 132,608 → 137,216 bytes (+4.5 KB), all three symbologies encoding 197,120 → 204,288 (+7.0 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged, measured after the speed work below. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md).

**Lessons.**
- The plan's rule for `Optimal` ("Kanji runs ... taken when it lowers the version, as any plan is today") says nothing about the UTF-8 plan `Optimal` wrote before, and read literally it lets `Optimal` grow a symbol: a Kanji plan pays a header wherever a cell meets ASCII, so interleaved text can lose to one UTF-8 Byte run. Found by pricing 「1日2回3錠」 by hand before writing the scan, and pinned on all three symbologies. The exit criterion "`Optimal` never larger than `Single`" would not have caught it.
- Of the inventory's premises, the per-character price was the only screen term that decides. The narrowest-header terms (Micro QR's count indicator, rMQR's `MinCountBitsAny`) cannot, for the texts the Kanji scans see, because such a plan has at least two runs. So the exit criterion "a test where the old bound would have skipped the winning plan" has nothing to find there, and mutation checking agrees. rMQR's floor width and memo key do decide, and each has its test. The screen worth having for this text is a different one, a header per stretch, and it came from the benchmark, not from the inventory.
- A bound's first test can catch a fault for another reason than the bound. The first catch of the memo-key fault was a Kanji key colliding with a UTF-8 key of the same widths, and a key that keeps the two programs apart but drops Kanji's width went through, until a search under that fault found 「1日」×9 then 28 digits.
- Git Bash's `grep` does not see `\r`, so a CRLF check built on it reported CRLF for files that `sed -i` had turned to LF. `perl` counts them right.
- The seam from 6.3 widens: until 6.5, a text that fits one symbol as a Kanji plan under `Optimal` but not as UTF-8 comes out of `CreateStructuredAppend` as a UTF-8 set of two or more, while `Create` gives one symbol.

**Benchmark delta.** Base `e6555a6` against this change, both trees exported, ShortRun, three rounds alternating, median of three per arm, 152 arms. The set was the 6.3 set plus `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` (the walk back and the plan pricing changed) and `KanjiEncode`'s new `Optimal` arms: a text with ASCII in it under `Optimal`, beside the same text with UTF-8 asked for, copied into the base tree. That was more than the change could reach; the next phase narrows the set to the classes a change touches, with a few untouched arms for the noise. Allocation is identical on every arm. The untouched arms' class medians are −3.4 % to +1.5 %, overall −0.9 %, except `SimpleEncode` (+10.3 %) and `SimpleMicroQREncode` (+31.5 %). Those two were high in rounds 1 and 3 only and level in round 2, and in the narrowed probe below they came out 8-25 % faster in head, so they are the noise of that run.

The arms whose output moves:
- 「こんにちは世界、QRコードの分割テストです。」×3 as a Kanji plan (7-M, against 10-M) is faster than its UTF-8 twin: 3,140 ns against 3,647.
- 「日本7777」×10 was slower: Standard QR 2,983 ns against the UTF-8 twin's 2,361 (+26 %), rMQR 1,856 against 1,254 (+48 %), and Micro QR 「日本語12345」 322 against base's 261 (+23 %).

Timing each step in Release (Stopwatch, best of nine) showed where the difference was. The Kanji program is cheaper than the UTF-8 one (99 ns against 203 for 60 characters). The difference was:
- the analysis reading past ASCII, with a table lookup on each ASCII character (+90 ns);
- building a plan that wins (270-285 ns), where the UTF-8 twin builds none because its plan loses;
- rMQR's writer at 12-15 ns a run (20 runs here), a third of which was re-measuring the plan.

Three changes followed, all within this phase:
- the analysis tests ASCII before the lookup;
- the screens count a header per stretch (see "Done"), which spares Standard QR the 4-M cost run for this text;
- `MeasurePlan`, `PricePlan` and the Standard QR and rMQR writers look a version's count widths up once instead of per run, which also speeds every existing UTF-8 plan.

By Stopwatch, Standard QR then came out level (2,534 ns against 2,519) and rMQR at +22 % (1,562 against 1,282).

A narrowed probe confirmed it: 24 arms, three launches of fifteen iterations, base and head interleaved twice. The same base arm was 25-50 % apart between that probe's two runs, so each verdict pairs arms of the same run. Standard QR's Kanji plan was within noise of its UTF-8 twin (+5 %), the sentence faster, rMQR +20 %, and Micro QR +30 % against base. What remains on rMQR is a second table lookup per character (the analysis and the writer each look every character up) and a second cost run (the scan's runs keep no predecessors, so the build runs the program again with them). Decided with the user on 2026-09-30: that work goes to 6.8, which therefore lands before the release; the row above says so.

### 6.5 Structured Append (2026-09-30)

**Done.** `CreateStructuredAppend` analyses the text as `Create` does (`allowKanji` unless a byte order mark is asked for, `planKanji` under `Optimal`), and an eligible text can be a Kanji set: no ECI header in any symbol, and the parity `StructuredAppendPlanner.ParityKanji`, the XOR of the whole text's Shift_JIS bytes computed from the reverse table's 13-bit values (ISO/IEC 18004 8.4.5 run backwards). The rules are the plan's:
- under `Single` a set is a Kanji set only when every character has a cell, each chunk one Kanji segment;
- under `Optimal` a text with ASCII in it is a Kanji set, each chunk its Kanji plan with no UTF-8 fallback, only when that needs fewer symbols than today's UTF-8 set or as many at a lower version (ties keep today's set);
- a text of every-cell characters is a Kanji set under both segmentations without the comparison, a decision made here: the plan's `Optimal` row reads as if it applied to every eligible text, but for this class the Kanji set is never larger (13 bits a character against 16 or 24 and no ECI header, so any split of the UTF-8 set is a split of the Kanji set), and comparing would only let a tie make `Optimal` write UTF-8 where `Single` writes Kanji.

The planner gained a Kanji cost model under its unchanged three searches (`TryPlan(..., kanji: true)`, `TryPlanKanji`):
- `ChunkBitsKanji` is the definition: 20 bits and one Kanji segment, or 20 bits and the Kanji plan;
- `LongestChunkEndKanji` is the walk's step: a closed form under `Single`, and under `Optimal` one forward pass of a new eighth-state prefix walk, `ModeSegmenter.LongestPrefixWithinBudgetKanji`;
- `CheapestPayloadBitsKanji` is the rate bound, a cell at 13 bits, and the whole-text floor is the Kanji program's;
- the single-mode shortcuts (a mode that changes at most twice, a non-alphanumeric character extending only a Byte run) and `CanPlanHelp` are not taken for a Kanji set, whose chunks can hold both kinds of character; the inventory's `PlanCouldBeatSingleMode` / `PlanIsOneByteRun` / `oneRunPlans` belong to those shortcuts and so are not consulted.

K9: a Kanji set's walks and plans run scalar (`allowLanes: false` in the planner, no lane passes in `CreateKanjiSet`); the UTF-8 set it is compared with runs the seven-state program, lanes included. Which of the two sets is planned first, and whether the other is planned at all, is decided by their floors (`StructuredAppendPlanner.CanHoldKanji`, `FewestSymbols`); this was added after the benchmark, below. The one-symbol question is asked with `Create`'s analysis, which closes the seam 6.3 and 6.4 recorded: a text one symbol holds as Kanji or as a Kanji plan, and not as UTF-8, is now `Create`'s symbol rather than a UTF-8 set. The refusal's advice re-analyses the text when it tries another segmentation, so a text only a Kanji set holds is told to use `Optimal`. XML docs, `docs/migration.md` ("Structured Append sets follow the same rule", the parity bullet), the encoder record ("A Kanji-eligible text can be a Kanji set"), the architecture's rule and scope row, and the fixture matrix are updated; `PublicAPI.approved.txt` is unchanged.

**Verified.**
- `StructuredAppendKanjiTest`, 103 tests through the public API and the planner:
  - The parity equals the XOR of CP932's bytes, on the 6.4 corpus and cell by cell over every encoder cell (both Shift_JIS ranges), and is 176 for the CodeGlyphX text.
  - `ChunkBitsKanji` and `LongestChunkEndKanji` equal a reference that prices each chunk from `KanjiPlanReference` or from the standard's definition.
  - `TryPlanKanji` returns the reference walk's three answers: the fewest symbols at the largest version, the smallest version holding that many, and the smallest budget (the balanced bound).
  - Every-cell texts are Kanji sets under both segmentations, written out symbol by symbol from `KanjiStreamReference` with the mask pinned, and never larger than their UTF-8 set.
  - Texts with ASCII in them are Kanji sets under `Optimal` exactly where the reference says the set is smaller; otherwise, and under `Single`, the set equals the one with UTF-8 asked for, module for module. Both outcomes occur in the table.
  - A one-symbol result equals `Create`, also at the last bit (seven cells in 103 of version 1-Q's 104 bits).
  - The boost prices the Kanji streams, also where the fullest chunk fills 123 of the next level's 128 bits.
  - K9: `TryPlanKanji` runs no lane batch and the writer no lane pass, where the same text asked for as UTF-8 does on a machine with lanes.
  - The refusal counts Kanji characters, and under `Single` advises `Optimal` where only a Kanji set holds the text.
  - For the CodeGlyphX text at M with versions up to 3: `Optimal` writes 176 and `Single` writes 6.
  - `CanHoldKanji` never refuses a count the reference walk reaches, at five versions over the planner corpus, and its stretch term decides to the bit: 「a日b本c」 × 12 at 1-L needs 9 symbols, where the characters alone would admit 5.
  - Which sets are planned, counted (`KanjiSetPlans`, `Utf8SetPlans`): 「a日b本c」 × 200 plans no Kanji set, and the CodeGlyphX sentence × 45 no UTF-8 set. Over 800 seeded texts of short units where kanji, digits and letters take turns, and five fixed ones, the set is the one planning both would choose, each set is planned at most once, a text `Create` holds in one symbol is that symbol, and all eight ways the planning can go occur (which set first; the other skipped by its count, by its version, or planned and taken or not).
- `ModeSegmenterKanjiParityTest`: `LongestPrefixWithinBudgetKanji` stops where `KanjiPlanReference`'s prefix costs do. It runs on the corpus texts of up to 120 characters, at every width shape, with budgets at each prefix's cost and one bit either side.
- `StructuredAppendZXingCrossTest` gained three Kanji sets (Japanese with ASCII under `Optimal`, every-cell text under `Single` and under `Optimal` with the boost). ZXing.Net reassembles all 12 rows and reports the Shift_JIS parity.
- One existing test moved as intended: `Set_WhoseFirstChunkIsItsShortest_IsWritten`'s text is every-cell, so with the charset left to the library it is now a Kanji set of 11 symbols instead of a UTF-8 set of 13. It now runs both ways, with UTF-8 asked for as the old row.
- `spot-check-structured-append`: 189 symbols read by the three readers, 18 parity comparisons, 0 mismatches. The Japanese case under `Optimal` is now a Kanji set of 2 symbols at 4-M. It carries 176, the value CodeGlyphX's Kanji set carries and not the UTF-8 oracle's 6, so the tool now accepts the Shift_JIS parity for such a set. The other 17 comparable parities equal the oracle's.
- Byte-identical: the 6.4 harness against `807d8f4` and this change, 52,716 cases over 754 texts. ASCII, Latin-1, empty and no-cell text: 0 differences. The differences are all Structured Append size lines and refusal messages:
  - Every-cell text: 44 in all. `Optimal` has 18 sets with fewer symbols and 3 refusal messages; `Single` has 19 with fewer symbols, 2 that fit where they did not, and 2 refusal messages.
  - Eligible text with ASCII under `Optimal`: 46 sets with fewer symbols, 3 that fit where they did not, 3 with as many symbols at a lower version, and 3 refusal messages.
  - Eligible text with ASCII under `Single`: 4 refusal messages only, whose advice now names `Optimal`.

  No set grew, none stopped fitting, and no tie changed. The same harness against the tree after the planning order below gives the same 52,716 results, file for file.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 23 faults:
  - the parity: the second range's offset, the byte split, the 0xC0 radix;
  - the cost model: the rate bound, Kanji's count width in the chunk price and in the walk, the 13-bit step, the walk's budget, the whole-text floor, `Single`'s one-symbol bound, the lanes, the segmentation the searches run;
  - the prefix walk: its budget comparison, and a Byte run of ASCII extending over a cell;
  - the generator: the tie rule, every-cell text skipping the comparison, the skip of the UTF-8 set, the one-symbol word taken from the UTF-8 set, the analysis's two flags, the boost, the refusal's re-analysis, and the writer's plan check.

  19 were caught on the first pass. The four survivors:
  - The parity's second range (0xE040 and up) at the first range's offset: the corpus checked against CP932 had no such cell. The cell-by-cell parity test catches it.
  - `Single`'s one-symbol bound at 14 bits a character: the one-symbol test had room to spare. The last-bit test catches it.
  - The boost priced 8 bits high: no case sat within a byte of the next level. The 123-of-128 case catches it.
  - Lanes for a Kanji set: equivalent, since the only caller passes `allowLanes: false`. The redundant condition is gone, a `Debug.Assert` states the rule, and a fault that passes `allowLanes: true` from `TryPlanKanji` is caught by 3 tests.

  The re-run catches all four.
- The planning order, added after the benchmark, was checked on its own with 17 faults: the order, each skip's count clause and version clause, the version below and the range's minimum, the one-symbol bound on the skip, the Kanji floor's stretch term and its width, and `FewestSymbols`'s limit. 12 were caught on the first pass. The range's minimum and the one-symbol bound (three faults) needed texts the random corpus did not produce; a search found 「123a本a123」 at 1-Q, whose UTF-8 set sits at the lowest version the range allows, and 「日123本aa999」 at 2-H, one symbol as a Kanji plan (126 of 128 bits) but not as UTF-8 (136), whose Kanji set is skipped. As fixed cases they catch all three. The other two are equivalent: `FewestSymbols` stopping at 16 instead of reporting 17 changes a floor only where 16 symbols of the largest version cannot hold the text, and the version clause then skips the same set.

**Trimmed size.** Against `807d8f4`, `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: a consumer that calls `CreateStructuredAppend` 161,792 → 165,888 bytes (+4.0 KB), QR encode only 137,216 unchanged, all three symbologies encoding 204,288 → 204,800 (+0.5 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md).

**Benchmark delta.** Base `807d8f4` against this change, both trees exported with the head's benchmark sources, narrowed to what the change reaches: `KanjiEncode` (its `Create` arms are the noise reference) and eight `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode` shapes, with `byte-4k-max10` and `mixed-40k-any` as ASCII controls. ShortRun, three rounds alternating, median of three, 42 arms, 33 minutes; the first attempt, three launches of fifteen iterations over every shape, would have taken three hours and was stopped. `utf8-15k-*` now ask for UTF-8, which leaves their output as it was. The same texts with the charset left to the library are the new `kanji-15k-*`, and `cells-15k-any` / `cells-15k-utf8` are an every-cell text and its UTF-8 twin. Allocation is identical wherever the output did not change.

The Structured Append arms against forced UTF-8, each against its twin in the same run of head (the label-sized ones from three launches of fifteen iterations, twice):
- 1,000 cells at versions up to 10-L, `Single`: the Kanji set (7 symbols) 29.5 µs against 44.2 for the UTF-8 set (12), −33 %, with 3.3 KB allocated against 5.7.
- 1,000 characters of the CodeGlyphX sentence, `Optimal`: 36.1 µs (7 symbols) against 40.7 (11), −11 %.
- 15,000 every-cell characters at any version: 582 µs under `Single` and 600 under `Optimal` (9 symbols of version 39) against 1,004 and 1,031 (16 of 40), −42 %.
- `kanji-15k-any` under `Optimal`: 682-735 µs (9 symbols) against 934-969 for `utf8-15k-any` (15), about −25 %. `kanji-15k-mixed`: 613 µs (7 of version 39) against 771-994 (10 of 40), −20 % or more.
- Where the Kanji set loses, 「a日b本c」 × 200 at versions up to 10-L under `Optimal`, whose set is the UTF-8 set: 28.6 µs against 27.0 for the same set asked for as UTF-8, +6 %, which is the analysis reading past ASCII and the floors' one pass. Before the floors it was 39.5 against 27.1, +46 % (see Lessons).

The gain is the symbol count. A Kanji set's planning runs scalar (K9) and is still the smaller share: 2 % over its symbols for the every-cell text under `Single`, where the UTF-8 set's planning with lanes is 8 %. So for sets the scalar path meets 6.8's "no slower than forced UTF-8" bar, except the losing case's +6 %, which is the analysis and not the lanes.

Base against head on the arms whose output did not change: `KanjiEncode`'s `Create` arms −10.2 % to +3.5 %, the forced-UTF-8 set arms −6.8 % to +1.8 %, the ASCII controls −4.6 % to −0.8 %. Two arms were outliers, and neither path changed. `RmQR_Utf8Plan_Mixed_Encode` was +49 % in ShortRun, but level with base in three launches of fifteen iterations (base 1,261 and 1,144 ns, head 1,242 and 1,147). The `Symbols` arm of `mixed-40k-any` was +39 %: one launch in three ran at 2.3 times the others, a bimodality the same arm's base showed in 6.4.

**Lessons.**
- Telling a Kanji set from a UTF-8 set by its parity failed first: a text repeated an even number of times XORs to 0 in both charsets. The tests compare modules with the set asked for as UTF-8, and the corpus repeats odd counts.
- A reference that checks a table-driven computation has to reach every range of the table. The 6.4 corpus was written for costs, and none of its cells sat in Shift_JIS's second range, so the parity's second offset went untested until the mutation check.
- K9's zero meant nothing at first: the UTF-8 set a Kanji set is compared with runs lanes, so a lane counter over `CreateStructuredAppend` was not 0. The test measures the Kanji planner and the Kanji writer on their own.
- The plan's `Optimal` rule compares every eligible text with its UTF-8 set. For every-cell text that comparison can only lose a tie, so it is not made.
- A comparison has to be benchmarked where it loses too. The first twin arms were all texts whose Kanji set wins, and they read as a clean gain. An arm where it loses (interleaved text, whose set stays UTF-8) showed +46 % over forced UTF-8, because the Kanji set was planned in full before it lost. The floors now decide which set is planned first and skip the one that cannot win. The random-corpus test holds that the skips never change the set, and the counters that they happen.

### 6.6 Interop and fixtures (2026-10-01)

**Done.** No library code changed: this phase is fixtures, tests, the interop tool and the record.
- Fixtures, regenerated with the pinned generators (qrtool fetched and checked by `get-qrtool.ps1`):
  - Standard QR, ZXing.Net: two Kanji cases in the 12-bit count band, `kanji-v27-edge-m` (653 characters, one past what version 26-M holds) and `kanji-v40-max-l` (1,817, version 40-L filled).
  - rMQR, qrtool: four Kanji cases at the widths the corpus had left to derivation, each filled to the version's Kanji capacity: R7x43-M (3 characters, a 2-bit count), R7x59-M (6) and R9x43-H (3) at 3 bits, and R9x139-M (38) at 6 bits. All four are under 11 modules high, clear of qrtool's tail defect.

  The new payloads cycle through cells that include the edges of both Shift_JIS ranges (0x8140, 0x9FFC, 0xE040, 0xEAA4). The rest of the corpus came out byte for byte as committed; the generator writes LF, so the working tree showed 618 files modified until they were compared with `--ignore-cr-at-eol` and restored.
- `KanjiEncoderOracleTest` makes the Kanji fixtures an encoder oracle. A single Kanji segment at a fixed version and level has one valid stream, so this library's symbol of the fixture's text must equal the fixture module for module. The mask is pinned to the one the manifest records (ZXing.Net's own report; the zxing-cpp gate's reading for qrtool's Micro QR), and rMQR has one. qrtool's rMQR tail modules are left out. The divergent-cell fixture is left out by name, since its text has no encoder cells. The test also requires the fixtures to cover every Kanji count width (Standard QR 8, 10 and 12; Micro QR 3 and 4; rMQR 2 to 7), and the filled ones to hold exactly the count this library holds there. `KanjiFixtureTest`'s floors rose to 7 Standard QR and 8 rMQR fixtures.
- `spot-check-kanji`, new in `tools/QRInteropFixtures`, reads this library's Kanji output with every pinned reader of each symbology:
  - every encoder cell, in chunks, in Standard QR at 1-L, 13-L and 27-L (one version per count band), Micro QR at M3-L and M4-L, and rMQR at R7x43-M, R7x59-M, R9x139-M and R17x139-M (counts of 2, 3, 6 and 7 bits);
  - ASCII `\` and `~` in Byte runs beside Kanji runs under `Optimal`, each text confirmed a Kanji plan before it counts (zxing-cpp's raw bytes are its Shift_JIS encoding);
  - a Kanji segment after ECI 26, for 6.7. This library does not write one, so these symbols come from QrCodeGenerator 3.2.1, whose `DataSegment.MakeSegment` and `MakeECISegment` build a symbol from explicit segments with a Kanji table of its own.
- Specs: the fixture spec's corpus counts, consuming tests, probe list and a new oracle-matrix row; rMQR's Kanji widths (read from qrtool symbols now, not only derived); the architecture's "No Kanji beside an ECI header" with the measurement; K4 and the 6.7 row. The 2.0.0 plan's Phase 8 checklist now lists the spot checks with the results they last gave, and the Kanji symbols for the physical scanner pass.

**Verified.**
- `KanjiEncoderOracleTest`, 24 tests. Test-first: before the new fixtures, the coverage tests failed on Standard QR's 12-bit band and rMQR's widths 2, 3 and 6. The 13 existing Kanji fixtures (Standard QR 5, Micro QR 5, rMQR 3) equalled this library's symbols on the first run. With the fixtures, all 19 comparisons pass, and every filled count is the last one this library holds (Standard QR's band edge: the text does not fit version 26, and one character fewer does).
- `spot-check-kanji`, 2026-10-01:
  - Every encoder cell was read back exactly by every reader. Standard QR: 18 symbols, by this library, zxing-cpp, ZXing.Net and CodeGlyphX. Micro QR: 917 symbols, and rMQR: 200, by this library and zxing-cpp. ZXing.Net found one 27-L symbol in its image only with the pure-barcode hint; that is finding the symbol, not reading it. No JIS X 0208 row loses its cells under K7.
  - `\` and `~` in Kanji plans were read as themselves by every reader of all three symbologies, none as JIS X 0201's ¥ and ‾, so they stay in Kanji plans' Byte runs. One text came out UTF-8 in Standard QR, where the Kanji plan does not lower the version, and is reported without counting.
  - After ECI 26, this library, ZXing.Net and CodeGlyphX read the Kanji segment as JIS X 0208. zxing-cpp 0.5.2 decodes its Shift_JIS bytes as UTF-8: 「日本語」 comes back as U+FFFD, U+FFFD, `{`, U+FFFD, U+FFFD in each of the four arrangements tried (the `{` is 0x7B, the second byte of 本's Shift_JIS 0x967B). With the Kanji segment ahead of the ECI it comes back as ISO-8859-1 instead. The reason is in zxing-cpp's `Content::switchEncoding`: once a symbol has an ECI, the charset a Kanji segment sets is dropped, and bytes ahead of the first ECI default to ISO-8859-1, so no order of segments avoids it. The same segment with no ECI, which is what this library writes, is read by all four. 6.7's condition is therefore not met, and 6.7 is not taken.
- The other spot checks, run again: `spot-check-microqr` 18 of 18, `spot-check-rmqr` 444 of 444, `spot-check-structured-append` 189 symbols, 18 parity comparisons, 0 mismatches.
- The fixture-driven suites pass with the new fixtures (`*Fixture*` 1,190 tests, `RmQR*` 4,712, `MicroQR*` 1,252), and so does the whole suite (net10.0 16,150, net8.0 16,137).

**Decision: 6.7 is not taken (with the user, 2026-10-01).** zxing-cpp's reading looked at first like one reader's quirk, so readers and the standard were surveyed before deciding:
- **The standard is on zxing-cpp's side.** ISO/IEC 18004:2015 treats data under an ECI as byte values that may be compacted in whatever mode suits (7.4.2.1), and Kanji mode as a compaction of Shift_JIS-range byte pairs (7.3.6, Annex H); the ECI in force interprets every byte that follows. A Kanji segment after ECI 26 therefore means UTF-8 bytes, not JIS X 0208 characters, and 6.7's symbols would not mean what they were written to mean. Nothing forbids Kanji after an ECI; the text simply assumes this reading. ZXing's maintainer keeps the other reading on purpose (zxing/zxing#1498, closed unmerged in 2022); zxing-cpp's maintainer, BWIPP's author and an ISO participant hold the standard's.
- **Readers split, open and closed.** Kanji read as JIS X 0208 whatever the ECI: ZXing and its ports (ZXing.Net, zxing-js, gozxing), BoofCV, jsQR, rxing by default, and by a third party's report Google ML Kit and Scandit. The ECI governs Kanji: zxing-cpp, ZBar, and by the same report Cognex, Zebra and Alipay. quirc, OpenCV and WeChat's engine return raw bytes.
- **Such symbols are rare.** No mainstream encoder writes Kanji after an ECI other than 20 by default (BWIPP did until bwip-js turned it off in 4.4.0; zint only with `--fullmultibyte`), and zxing-cpp's maintainer found none among about 200 symbols from the web.
- **Kanji with no ECI, which 6.3-6.5 write, reads the same on both sides**: every reader that decodes text reads it as Shift_JIS, zxing-cpp included. Strictly, the default interpretation has been ISO-8859-1 since the 2006 edition, and zint warns on Kanji without ECI 20. ECI 20 would settle that at 12 bits a symbol, and Google ML Kit's documentation lists QR codes "generated in the ECI mode" among those it does not recognize. The output stays as it is.
- **Phones, by hand (2026-10-01).** Six symbols were scanned from a screen: Kanji with no ECI; ECI 26 over a UTF-8 Byte segment alone (this library's output for such text); and the four arrangements of ECI 26 and Kanji above. The iPhone Camera app (iOS 26.5) read all six as written, so it reads Kanji as JIS X 0208 whatever the ECI, as ZXing does, and reads ECI 26 UTF-8. A phone that reads 6.7's symbols does not change the decision, which rests on the standard's reading and on the readers that follow it. A second page added ECI 20 before Kanji (alone and before ASCII), Shift_JIS in a Byte segment with no ECI and behind ECI 20, and Micro QR in Kanji and in UTF-8. On iPhone, the Camera app, Google Lens and 「QRを読む」 read the four Standard QR symbols, and none of them reads Micro QR at all. **Android 17 read only ECI 26 UTF-8.** Its QR scanner returned nothing readable for every Shift_JIS-based symbol (Kanji with or without ECI 20, Shift_JIS bytes with or without ECI 20), Google Lens on Android read none of them, and neither found the Micro QR symbols. So Kanji mode, the default 6.3-6.5 gave Standard QR, is unreadable on Android's own scanners, and ECI 20 does not rescue it. That reverses K2 for Standard QR (6.6a, decided with the user the same day): UTF-8 by default, Kanji when the caller asks, since industrial readers may want it. Micro QR and rMQR are not read by either phone, so their defaults are decided by Denso Wave's own reader (「クルクル - QRコードリーダー」), which reads both. On iPhone it read all seven symbols of a third page: Standard QR in Kanji and in ECI 26 UTF-8, rMQR in Kanji, in ECI 26 UTF-8 and as a Kanji plan beside digits, and Micro QR in Kanji (M3) and in UTF-8 with no ECI (M4, written by qrtool).

A text with a character that has no cell stays UTF-8, as it has since 6.3.

**Lessons.**
- An oracle that does not write what is being asked about can still build it. QrCodeGenerator 3.x takes explicit segments, which gave the tool a Kanji segment after ECI 26 without reaching into this library's internals, and with a Kanji table that is not this library's.
- A reader check has to confirm what it is reading. The first `\` and `~` texts were short, and in Standard QR and Micro QR they came out UTF-8, because the Kanji plan did not lower the version. They read back correctly and would have passed, while proving nothing about Kanji plans. The check now requires zxing-cpp's raw bytes to be the text's Shift_JIS encoding, and requires each symbology to have carried both characters in a Kanji plan.
- An image reader's miss can be about finding the symbol. ZXing.Net's one miss was a 27-L image it found only with the pure-barcode hint. The tool retries with the hint and reports how often it had to, so a detection miss is not counted as a misread cell.

**Trimmed size and benchmark.** No file under `src/` changed, so neither moved, and no benchmark was run.

### 6.6a UTF-8 by default, Kanji on request (2026-10-01)

**Why.** The phone scan of 6.6 (see its Decision) found that an Android 17 phone's own QR scanner and Google Lens on it read no Shift_JIS-based text at all: Kanji mode with no ECI, with ECI 20, or Shift_JIS in a Byte segment. They read the same text as UTF-8 behind ECI 26, and the iPhone apps read every form. A default that Android's own scanners misread is not a default. So, decided with the user: UTF-8 by default on all three symbologies, and Kanji mode only when the caller asks, since an industrial reader may want it.

Micro QR and rMQR were weighed separately, because neither phone's own scanner reads them. Denso Wave's reader (「クルクル - QRコードリーダー」, on iPhone) and zxing-cpp read both symbologies in Kanji mode and in UTF-8 alike, so nothing measured sets them apart from Standard QR. The other encoders split too: of the ten in the reference checkouts, CodeGlyphX, zint (zxing-cpp's writer), goban and rmqrcode-python write Kanji by default where they write it at all; QRCoder, QrCodeGenerator, go-qr and the Rust qrcode crates write UTF-8; and ZXing.Net loses the text to ISO-8859-1. One rule for all three is the simpler contract, so Micro QR follows it too (K5 revised).

**Done.**
- `AllowKanji` (bool, off by default) on `QRCodeGeneratorOptions`, `MicroQRCodeGeneratorOptions` and `RmQRCodeGeneratorOptions`, last in each, with a constructor parameter of the same name.
  - The analysis takes it as its `allowKanji` argument on every path: sizing, version and level resolution, the encode, both `Optimal` entries, the Structured Append analysis and the refusal's re-analysis. On Standard QR a byte order mark still overrides it.
  - The explicit-parameter internals (`CreateCore` and `PrepareConfiguration` in each generator, and rMQR's `Optimal` chain) carry it as a parameter.
- The option sits beside `EciMode` rather than in it. `EciMode`'s values are the ECI assignments written into the symbol; Kanji mode writes none. Its explicit members force a charset on every text, while Kanji can only be permitted, since ASCII, é, emoji and the seven divergent cells have no cell. None of the ten encoders surveyed puts Kanji mode with no ECI in a charset enum: ZXing.Net, zxing-cpp and QrCodeGenerator offer Shift_JIS as a charset (QrCodeGenerator and zint then write ECI 20 and Kanji), and QrCodeGenerator (`KanjiStrategy`) and CodeGlyphX keep Kanji as a control of its own.
- The XML docs of the three options, the generators, `EciMode` and the segmentation enums say Kanji mode is written on request, and why it is off.
- `PublicAPI.approved.txt` changes by three constructor signatures and three properties. The Playground's API page is regenerated. The Playground gained a "Kanji mode for Japanese text" checkbox (off, as in the library) for all three symbologies. It reaches the preview, both benchmark modes and the share link, whose older links leave it as it is. The UI still offers no charset or segmentation choice, so it shows single-mode Kanji only.
- `docs/migration.md`: "Japanese text is written in Kanji mode" becomes "Kanji mode on request: `AllowKanji`", an addition; the 2.0.0 summary no longer counts Kanji as a behaviour change.
- Specs: the architecture's "When Kanji mode is written" (only on request, and why), its scope row, and the encoder and decoder records.
- The tools' Kanji spot checks ask for the option, and `spot-check-structured-append` gained `kanji` and `kanji-opt` variants. `KanjiEncode`'s Kanji arms ask for it, and Micro QR gained UTF-8 twins (`MicroQR_Utf8_Encode`, `MicroQR_Utf8Plan_Encode`), which it can have now. `QRCodeStructuredAppendEncode`'s `kanji-15k-*` and `cells-15k-any` ask for it too.

**Verified.**
- Byte for byte, through the 6.5 harness (52,716 cases over 754 texts, every entry point, sizing and refusal of all three symbologies):
  - without the option, this change against the `2.0.0-preview.3` tag: identical, file for file;
  - with the option on every case, against 6.5's run: identical.

  `src/` changed nothing else since the tag, so these are the two exit criteria as stated.
- `KanjiEligibilityTest` gained the `AllowKanji` axis: each Kanji row with the option, its default twin (UTF-8 as before, Micro QR's bare UTF-8, a text past Micro QR's UTF-8 capacity refused), the option ignored under an explicit charset and under a byte order mark, sizing against Create in all eight combinations of segmentation, mark and option, a version range, the boost, and the refusals' units and wording. The Kanji test classes (`KanjiOptimalTest`, `StructuredAppendKanjiTest`, `KanjiEncoderOracleTest`, `KanjiZXingCrossTest`, the Kanji boundary in `QRCodeGeneratorVersionBoundaryTest`) now ask for the option.
- The tests 6.3 and 6.4 had moved to Kanji expectations are back to the earlier ones by default, with the Kanji case kept beside them under the option: Micro QR's round trip (「こんにちは」 M4 by default, M3 with the option), rMQR's exhaustive version reference and 「日本語1234567890」 (R11x43 by default, R13x27 with the option), and the Structured Append stream test's Japanese set (13 symbols by default, 11 with the option). `TypeShapeTest` holds each constructor parameter to its property.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 37 faults in the plumbing. Each of the option's call sites was turned to `true` (Kanji leaking into the default) and to `false` (the option ignored), with the byte order mark's override dropped, and the explicit-parameter chains broken. 33 were caught on the first pass. The four survivors were paths no test took with the right option: the refusal's re-analysis without the option, Standard QR's version resolution under a range or the boost without it, and Micro QR's ranged sizing either way. `Refusal_WithoutAllowKanji_DoesNotAdviseAKanjiSet`, the range and boost rows of `StandardQr_AllCellsByDefault_IsUtf8` and `MicroQr_RangedSizing_FollowsTheOption` catch them on the re-run. Two pairs of identical lines (the two Standard QR `Optimal` analyses, and Micro QR's two calls into `PrepareConfiguration`) cannot be mutated one at a time; the faults at the lines they call into, and in the helper both use, are caught.
- `spot-check-kanji`, `spot-check-microqr` (18 of 18), `spot-check-rmqr` (444 of 444) and `spot-check-structured-append` (275 symbols, 30 parity comparisons, 0 mismatches) pass. The Japanese set is the UTF-8 set again by default, parity 6 as the oracle writes, and the 4-M Kanji set with parity 176 under `kanji-opt`.
- The Playground, by hand from a Debug publish, as the verification list above asks.
  - Each symbology shrinks with the checkbox and decodes back to the input either way, in the classic style: Standard QR 「こんにちは世界」 at L goes from 2 to 1, rMQR the same text at M from R13x43 to R11x43, Micro QR 「こんにちは」 at L from M4 to M3.
  - A share link made with the box ticked restores it, and the symbol, on reload.
  - The encode-only benchmark writes M3 with it and M4 without.
  - The console shows no errors.

**Trimmed size.** Against `2c3214d`, `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: QR encode only 137,216 unchanged, all three symbologies encoding 204,800 → 205,312 bytes (+0.5 KB), a consumer that calls `CreateStructuredAppend` 165,888 → 166,400 (+0.5 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged. The option is read at run time, so a consumer that never sets it keeps the Kanji code as before; the half kilobyte is the option's plumbing. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md).

**Benchmark delta.** Base `2c3214d` (Kanji by default) against this change, narrowed to what it reaches: the three `Simple*Encode` classes, since every `Create` path now carries the option, and `KanjiEncode`, whose Kanji arms write the same symbol in both trees (by default in base, with the option in head). ShortRun, three rounds alternating, median of three, 67 arms, 55 minutes. Allocation is identical on every arm both trees have.
- The machine was noisy. The other libraries' arms, the same code in both trees, moved −24 % to +22 %; this library's moved −26 % to +10 % in `KanjiEncode` and −24 % to +17 % in the `Simple*Encode` classes, most of both kinds faster in head, which nothing here explains.
- Three of this library's arms were past +10 %: `QR_KanjiSet_Sentence_Encode` (+10.1 %), Micro QR's alphanumeric M3 (+13.7 %) and rMQR's numeric R7x43 (+16.5 %). Their rounds overlapped base's. Three launches of fifteen iterations, base and head interleaved twice, put each level with base: the Kanji set 40.4 and 43.5 µs in base against 40.5 and 41.6 in head, M3 193 and 187 ns against 207 and 182, R7x43 176 and 174 ns against 170 and 176.
- The new Micro QR twins, head only: 「こんにちは」 in UTF-8 (M4-L) 253 ns against 213 in Kanji mode (M3-L); 「日本語12345」 under `Optimal`, the UTF-8 plan (M4-L) 248 ns against 343 for the Kanji plan (M3-L).

**Lessons.**
- The interop measurement that mattered was a phone in a hand. Every library reader agreed with the Kanji output, the standard was on Kanji's side for the no-ECI form, and the default still had to go: Android's own scanners read none of it. A default is judged by the readers people have, so a phone scan belongs before an output default changes, not after.
- Opting in has to reach every path that analyses the text, and the paths the tests take by default are not all of them. The first mutation pass found three of them without a test: the refusal's advice, version resolution under a range or the boost, and Micro QR's ranged sizing.

### 6.8 Kanji plan speed (2026-10-01)

**Why.** 6.4 left a Kanji plan on interleaved text slower than its UTF-8 twin (rMQR +20 %, Micro QR +30 % against the build before Kanji plans) and named two remedies: the scan's cost run reused for the build, and one reverse-table lookup per character. K9's lanes were to gain the Kanji state only if the scalar path missed the bar.

**Measured first.** Each step in Release, timed in a harness against the library's internals (best of nine batches after a second's warm-up), on `KanjiEncode`'s texts before any change:
- Micro QR 「日本語12345」 at L: 304 ns as a Kanji plan (M3), 224 for the same text without the option. That twin plans nothing: its UTF-8 plan cannot win, so it is the single stream at M4. The Kanji path's analysis took 17 ns against 8, its scan 30 against 18, its build 37, its segmented writer 32.
- rMQR 「日本7777」×10 at M: 1,520 ns against 1,209 for UTF-8 asked. Analysis 70 against 15, 36 of it the 20 lookups. The scan 358 against 431. The build 222: the program with predecessors 151, the walk back 25, the counts 13, the measure 22. The writer 167.
- Standard QR, the same text: 2,493 against 2,322. The scan 241 against 355, the build 262.
- What accepts decides whether a run can be reused. Standard QR accepts on the band's cost run, whose widths are every version's in the band, and Micro QR on the candidate's own run. rMQR accepts R17x77 on the floor plan's upper bound, after cost runs at R15x77 and R13x99 turned those down, so no run exists at the version taken.

**Done.**
- `ShiftJisKanjiReverseTable.HasCell`, emitted by the table generator: the lookup's directory and membership word, without the rank and the value. The analysis asks it, so the writer's is the one value lookup per character. The regenerated table differs by that method only.
- Standard QR and Micro QR: the Kanji scan writes each Kanji cost run's predecessors into a table the generator lends, and hands back the accepting run's end state and cost; `TryBuildKanjiPlan` has an overload that walks that table back. The table is on the stack for short text and pooled past 256 characters on Standard QR, and 70 bytes on Micro QR; a text with no Kanji plan gets none. Sizing keeps the path without a table, and both reach the same version.
- rMQR and Micro QR price a Kanji plan in one pass that also fills each run's count (`PriceKanjiPlan`), as Standard QR's `PricePlan` already did. Every count is the run's length, since a Kanji plan's Byte runs hold only ASCII. Micro QR's `MeasurePlan` looks its headers up once per version, Kanji's from M3 only.
- K9: the lanes do not gain the Kanji state (the row above).
- Specs: the Standard QR encoder record (the membership test, the build from the scan's table), the rMQR encoder record (why its build runs the program itself), the Micro QR spec map, and the trimmed sizes in the architecture.

**Verified.**
- `HasCell_AgreesWithLookup_EveryCodeUnit`: every UTF-16 code unit.
- `KanjiPlanTableReuseTest`, for Standard QR and Micro QR. The scan with a table chooses what it chooses without one, and the plan built from the table equals the plan the build makes alone, run for run. The texts are the Kanji parity corpus, random eligible texts, and short digits-cells-digits texts at M3-L's capacity, where the screen lets M3 through and its run turns it down (「3771。え字3146」: screen 83, plan 86, capacity 84). The test counts acceptances after an earlier candidate's run was turned down (M4 after M3, a later band after an earlier one), where a table kept from the first run would be wrong. The first corpus had too few of them on Micro QR; a search found the shape.
- Byte for byte through the 6.5 harness (52,716 cases), by default and with `AllowKanji`, against 6.6a's run: identical.
- The full suite: 32,373 tests over both frameworks.
- `tools/mutation_check.cs` planted 21 faults and every one was caught:
  - in the membership test, its bit and its record;
  - in the analysis, its test;
  - in the pricing, the count, the payload, the Kanji header, and Micro QR's header from M3;
  - in each hand-off of the table: the run kept, the end state, the cost, a table kept from an earlier candidate or band, the table's size, the walk's start.

  Micro QR's header from M3 is caught by `MeasurePlan`'s own test only: in Release the writer's re-measure only bounds the stream, and an underestimate passes it.

**Trimmed size.** Against `b0343f9`, `PublishTrimmed` with `TrimMode=full`, win-x64: QR encode only 137,216 → 138,240 bytes (+1.0 KB), all three symbologies encoding 205,312 → 206,848 (+1.5 KB), `CreateStructuredAppend` 166,400 → 167,424 (+1.0 KB), QR decode only 73,216 unchanged. Recorded in [qrcode-symbologies.md](../specs/qrcode-symbologies.md).

**Benchmark delta.** The machine was shared while this phase was measured: other sessions ran builds, tests, mutation runs and a busy loop. The ShortRun A/B was run twice: `KanjiEncode`, the Optimal arms of `QRCodeSegmentationEncode` and `MicroQRSegmentationEncode`, and FeatherQR's `SimpleEncode` arms as the noise reference, three rounds alternating. In both runs untouched arms moved −43 % to +37 %, in whichever tree a load fell on. The verdict therefore comes from base and head alternated in short processes, ABBA order: each arm the best of nine batches after a second's warm-up, ten processes (twelve for Micro QR). The noise arm moved +0.2 % and −0.3 %. Head against base, best and median:
- Kanji plans: Standard QR 「日本7777」×10 −3.6 % and −6.0 %, the sentence −3.5 % and −4.6 %; Micro QR 「日本語12345」 −12.7 % and −8.1 %; rMQR −2.4 % and −3.3 %.
- Paths without a Kanji plan, which the restructured generators reach: Standard QR's Optimal arms −0.3 % to −3.6 %. Micro QR's are within 2 %, except `mixed-8`, which read +6.8 % in the ten-process run and −5.2 % in the twelve-process one: an arm moves by about 6 % from one set of processes to the next.

The bar is still missed. Against the UTF-8 twin in the same processes, the Kanji plan is +4 % to +9 % on Standard QR, +12 % to +35 % on Micro QR and +6 % on rMQR. In the A/B's quiet rounds it is +10 to +12 %, +11 to +27 % and +25 %; the measurements disagree on rMQR's twin, not on the Kanji plan. What is left is the plan itself. On Micro QR the twin plans nothing, and on rMQR the build's run at the version taken is most of the difference, which nothing here removes. **Decided with the user on 2026-10-01: accepted.** Kanji mode is written only on request since 6.6a, and a caller who asks gets the smaller symbol (M3 for M4, R17x77 for R13x139) for a few tens of nanoseconds on Micro QR and a few hundred on rMQR.

**Lessons.**
- The remedies were named before anything was measured, and how far each could go turned on which filter accepts. Reuse pays only where a cost run accepts at the widths the build would use (Standard QR's band, Micro QR's candidate). rMQR's scan accepts on an upper bound and has no run to reuse. Step timings with the accepting filter traced said so in minutes, before any code moved.
- A harness's first measurements ran unoptimised code. A warm-up of 150,000 calls (about 15 ms) ended before tiered compilation's call-counting delay, so the items timed first read 3 to 10 times slower than the later ones, and a part could appear to cost more than the whole that contains it. A one-second warm-up fixed it.
- A shared machine needs a check before a benchmark, not after it. Two 40-minute A/Bs were lost to other sessions' builds, tests and mutation runs, a busy loop and leftover `grep` processes, which the CPU load (100 %) and the process list would have shown first. Short alternating processes with a noise arm survive drift that a three-round ShortRun does not.
- An arm compared across processes moves by about 6 % on this machine. A gain of 3-6 % is real only where several arms and both statistics agree.
